claims.claim: Reviewers note that some quests lack clear direction or bug out, requiring players to look up solutions externally.

citations.review_text:
I didn't realize until recently that this game runs on/uses the same engine as Star Wars KOTOR 1 and 2/Jade Empire & Neverwinter Nights. Given my brief personal knowledge of the Aurora Engine and how it reads files and scripts, I had to give this game a chance. I never was able to get into The Witcher 2 & 3, mostly because I didn't play enough of the first game to know enough about the story and its characters.

After recently playing through The Witcher 1, I can see why it has sequels. Not only is the first game a fresh take on the Aurora engine, but it's a decent RPG that is worth a play through. It feels alive and has plenty of narrative choice, and it also plays well with keyboard and mouse. With that said, I think its weakest parts are its quests and the day and night cycle that so many quests rely on. Some quests might glitch out and require you to look up the solution, even if it gives a quest marker/general idea of where to investigate. This mostly pertains to Chapter 2 and its Salamandar quests. After that the game seems to open up somewhat and doesn't lock you out of quest markers as much. There is a lot of backtracking too if you don't find shortcuts back to certain areas.

When I first played this game more than a decade ago, I didn't like the combat at all, but if you take into consideration that this game runs on an old engine from 2002 that was specifically made for DND RPGS, then you can at least appreciate it for what it is. It's quite addicting at times.

Combat is clunky and the quest design is flawed. There were many instances where the game gave me no direction at all, forcing me to search online to figure out what to do. Some quests can also get locked out if completed in the wrong order. Despite all this, I really enjoyed the story, atmosphere, and romance elements. Surprisingly, I didn’t encounter any game-breaking bugs or glitches, so I’d still highly recommend it to players who want to start their Witcher journey.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat system as timing-based, requiring players to click in rhythm to perform combos.

citations.review_text:
The first game, while incredibly janky at times and with a combat system that is basically a rhythm game in disguise, is still in my opinion the closest in atmosphere to the original 
books. The story definitely takes a bit too much from the books with how Alvin is basically a copy of Ciri, but the writing is still pretty good. The way this game forces you to make difficult choices and deal with the consequences, sometimes presented to you way after those choices have been made, is very impressive and unique in games even today. The witchering aspect of preparation before monster fights is also more meaningful than in the later games.

The Witcher feels old, but it has strong foundations.

After a short time, you notice the atmosphere. The world feels dark and grounded. Villages look poor. People fear monsters. The tone stays serious and mature from the start.

The combat system is unusual. You click to attack and time your clicks for combos. It feels strange at first. After some fights, you understand the rhythm. It becomes simple but satisfying.

The story pulls you in quickly. You play as Geralt with memory loss. This creates mystery from the beginning. Dialogues focus on politics, racism and moral conflict. Your choices already show consequences, even in early quests.

Graphics look outdated today. Animations feel stiff. Some character models repeat. Still, the soundtrack and sound design build strong immersion.

The game moves at a slower pace. You spend time reading quest logs and preparing potions while meditating. If you rush, you miss details.

After a few hours, you see its strength. It focuses on writing and world building. If you accept the old mechanics, you get a deep RPG with meaningful decisions.

The Atmospheric Cult Classic
The original Witcher is the definition of "acquired taste." Built on a heavily modified BioWare engine, it feels like a relic from a different era, yet it possesses a dark, Slavic atmosphere that many fans argue the sequels never quite replicated.

Combat: Rhythmic, Not Reactionary. Unlike modern action RPGs, the first game uses a timing-based "click-to-combo" system. You switch between three styles (Strong, Fast, Group), making combat feel like a lethal dance rather than a button-masher.

The World: It is grimy, rainy, and morally bankrupt. The game doesn't just tell you the world is dark; it makes you live in it through long, slow-burn chapters like the Vizima outskirts.

The "Slow" Burn: This is a 50-hour commitment. It rewards the patient player who enjoys reading bestiaries, gathering herbs, and actually being a Witcher.

Note for 2026: With the official remake currently in development, this original version serves as a fascinating historical document. It is the "purest" version of Geralt’s amnesia arc, though its technical limitations (frequent loading and dated animations) are undeniable.

Verdict: 8/10 — Essential for lore-buffs; mechanically divisive for everyone else.

The story, lorewise, is fantastic. It does a lot to immerse you into the story immediately, and gets you to care about the different characters you meet, and the goals of the protagonist in the game.

It looks like it was made by a political simpleton who thinks someone only acts racist when you say 'I hate ethnic group x and I think they should all die.' In the first act, you can sexually intimidate a barmaid, who ignores your attempts to seduce her. Then she, as 2 other female NPC's in the first act, gets surrounded by bandits, who plan to r*pe her. You kill the bandits, and now she (same as the other 2 scenario's), wants to have sex with you. You get a collectable card, as you do with every woman you sleep with in the game. It's done better in the books, but in the game, the female characters are very one-dimensional. How hard is it to write a woman? They're just like real people, you know.

All that said, I can't play this game seriously. I've had fun, but I just can't stop cringing about all the incel stuff.

claims.claim: The game lacks a fast travel system and mounts, forcing players to do extensive walking and backtracking across blocked-off environments.

citations.review_text: Played in 2026.Horribly dated.There's so much walking around and our traversal options are too limited.There's not even a jump or climb.You spent hours wasting time walking around (backtracking as well) just to get to the good parts.

TLDR for people who can't be bothered and want it fast: The game's not good. Plain and simple.

Now for the people who are curious as to the why... Well, there's plenty of reasons as to why:

First and foremost,this game does not respect your time at all.Not one damn bit. There's no fast travel,there's no mounts to use,there's not a shortcut you could take,because the genius designers  at CD PROJEKT RED decided that blocking half the sandbox with invisible walls so i have to take the long way around every single time i want to go from point A to point B is very good game design. I did discover recently into my errand boy runs that if i take the Crowd style stance,my Geralt moves faster. Guess what? DURING THE DAY WHILE WALKING AROUND YOU CANNOT USE IT(outside of scripted events and entering hostile places and all that jazz). Now to top it all off,there are no random encounters,monsters attacking you outside quests (back to those scripted events) and random encounters that would require you to fight.

Now let's get into the gameplay loop.Plain boring and repetitive to no end. You play a rythm game where you just have to time your attacks with the FLAMING SWORD. Use the signs twice a fight,and don't forget to spam potions i guess.

Some people would say this game just aged bad. Im here to tell you, it was never good. I mean at first i thought that this game was just old and some leniency was required. So i searched up when it appeared and what other games came in the year it was released. That happens to be 2007. Do you care to know what other games came in that year? Halo 3,Assassins Creed,Modern Warfare 4(When COD was still good),Bioshock,Crysis and quite a few other big titles. So honestly,that excuse is just not valid,because games that came out in the same year and quite a number that came before actually aged well and are still perfectly playable to this day,without any given leniency.

This was my first Witcher game, so I didn't have any attachment to the series or its characters. Maybe if you're already a Witcher fan, you'll enjoy it much more than I did.

For me, though, the game was just boring.

I actually didn't mind the graphics. Considering its age, they were decent, and I even appreciated some of the small details throughout the world.

My biggest issue was the combat. It became repetitive very quickly and never felt satisfying. I also couldn't really connect with the story, so it was hard to stay invested. On top of that, the game constantly sends you back and forth between locations, which made the pacing feel slow and tedious instead of engaging.

I can understand why some people consider this a classic, but unfortunately it just wasn't for me.

Great story and characters!
Just make sure you limit your GPU to 120 FPS max or the game will run wild! :)

Before you read this - if you have a modern PC (i.e. made after the year 2010) you need to FRAME LIMIT this game, or the fabric and hair physics will freak out, particuarly in menus and cutscenes. IDK why, I'm not a game developer, but it does fix the issue 99.9% of the time. 

A good, really interesting game that is in some ways unfortunately a product of its time. The Witcher is an action RPG of a now long bygone era, and is not exactly the most approachable to modern players. It demands patience (so much patience) to learn the mechanics, master the slightly strange combat mechanics, grind for 5000 gold to buy a single leather jacket...

The quests can be a little tedious as most of them are essentially just fetch quests as Geralt pursues his witcher work, killing various baddies in exchange for parts of those baddies in order to sell or present to a character to make some money. I will not lie. Or dying to another, extremely powerful for some reason, swamp monster. Or a cannibal and swamp monsters simultainiously.

+ Solid OST.
+ Decent graphics.

- Audio bugs.

The game is impossible to complete due to a bug, I can't rate it in a fair way.

Look.  If you play this expecting a modern RPG, you will be disappointed.  It is PEAK 00s.  The voice acting is terrible, the character modeling is also not great, and the character DESIGN for female characters is unequivocally awful.  

The narrative connective tissue is missing in a lot of places.  But it manages to be very fun nonetheless.  Once I got used to the janky-ass combat system, I liked it.  I think just... what it gets right, is the thing it needs to get right, which is to get the emotional highs in where it counts.  

I think the best synopsis I can give is to quote Roger Ebert's review of The Mummy:
"There is hardly a thing I can say in its favor, except that I was cheered by nearly every minute of it. I cannot argue for the script, the direction, the acting or even the mummy, but I can say that I was not bored and sometimes I was unreasonably pleased. There is a little immaturity stuck away in the crannies of even the most judicious of us, and we should treasure it."

Absolutely do not play this if you're expecting a 2020s-era RPG, but if you can handle a retro one, it does an admirable job.  I had a lot of fun playing it once I got used to the controls, despite all the jank.

I tried getting into The Witcher four times, over the past decade. This fourth time, it clicked.

The Witcher 1 plays a lot like Single Player RuneScape, if you were more quest focused. It demands the player to immerse themselves in the world, read everything, and talk to everyone, if you want to have all the information on how to handle situations. After the first hour Prologue tutorial, the game does not hold your hand. While there is a rhythm to the swordplay, I succeeded more on visual and sound effect cues. Frequently using the active pause, in Low Isometric Mode, I'd mix my combat style with my preference of bombs and spells, and a huge stack of potions. This made combat very tactical, and I eventually became a walking drugged-up mutant god.

Here are the main tips I'll give people, going in: 

1. Set your monitor and graphics card to 30 frames per second, while playing The Witcher. Mechanics begin to break above it. For example, your character chances to block and dodge are tied to framerate, through its tick system, and too many entities attacking you will fail to calculate your true damage mitigation at high frames. Not only would you move faster at 60 frames, but you'll also be twice as likely to die when surrounded. At 30 frames, sword fight timings are reasonable, and even the day/night cycle speeds, which are tied to your buff times, are fixed.

2. In fights involving NPC allies, do your best to protect them. If they die in most scenarios, they'd only be down-but-not-out, but sometimes they are your lifeline to win fights with ease.

3. Invest in resistance talents for Pain, Stun, and Knockdown. I didn't do this, and it made the game frustrating at times. All three of those things are Hard Crowd Control against you. Pain is especially terrible to face because there is not a single potion that can resist it.

4. You can stack certain food consumption buffs for rapid health regeneration without potion toxicity. They are not junk items, and sometimes, make…

Some technical issues aside (at least on newer hardware), FANTASTIC game. I played this for the first time about 10 years ago or so, and recently replayed after i had finally played the sequels too. I think most of us can agree Wild Hunt is the best of the trilogy due to the world building and immersion, but i still think this one has the best atmosphere of all The Witcher games, much of that due to the eerie soundtrack, especially during nighttime, you always feel like something's lurking behind every corner. 

This is also the most unique entry in the franchise in terms of gameplay, and this is exactly what divides people's opinions. Personally i love it, it took me some time getting used to when i first started playing this back then, and i almost gave up on it, but thank ♥♥♥♥ i continued and eventually figured it out, because once you do, it has a great medieval sword fighting combat system that's often overlooked, it's all about timing your attacks right. 

Last but not least, while i said Wild Hunt is the best in this regard, ALL 3 Witcher games are prime examples of how to build a great and immersive world, and this one especially is very close behind 3 in every aspect, including that. Every character in this franchise is extremely well written, even the unlikable ones. 

Now ofc it's based on the book series by Sapkowski, so that makes sense, but still. Best WRPG franchise by far, and i'd argue even my favorite RPG, or video game franchise in general now. Just peak, dark fantasy at its finest.
